Dwight Supplies $70M Refi on Newark Multifamily Tower
Developer Yisroel Berger seals fresh capital for newly redeveloped 25-story apartment building in New Jersey’s largest city
By Andrew Coen August 28, 2026 2:30 pm
reprintsNew Jersey developer Yisroel Berger has sealed a $70 million loan to refinance a newly redeveloped multifamily tower in Newark, N.J., Commercial Observer has learned.
A fund managed by Dwight Investment Management (formerly Dwight Mortgage Trust) provided the nonrecourse, interest-only loan for the 216-unit Cosmo 440 project in Newark’s South Ward neighborhood. The development previously received a $60 million loan from BridgeInvest last year for gut renovation of the building, which was constructed in 1969 and has sat empty for a decade, Jersey Digs reported at the time.
Dwight’s Alex Izso and David Scheer originated the loan.
“Cosmo 440 has revitalized Newark’s Southward, transforming a long-vacant tower into a stabilized, amenity-rich community well positioned near transit and Newark Liberty International Airport.” Izso and Scheer said in a statement.
Located at 440 Elizabeth Avenue, the 25-story building consists of 48 one-bedroom apartments, 120 two-bedroom units and 48 three-bedroom floor plans with 26 of the residences set aside as affordable housing. Community amenities include a concierge, coworking lounge, fitness center, playground and parking garage with electric vehicle charging.
Drew Capital’s Akiva Drew negotiated the debt for both loans.
“We’ve worked with the ownership and the property from the construction phase, through lease-up and now into its next stage of financing,” Drew, founder and principal of Drew Capital, said in a statement. “Executing successfully requires understanding every dimension of the deal.”
Berger did not immediately return a request for comment.
Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

Cortland Sells West Palm Rental at Discount for $208M
The transaction ranks among South Florida’s largest multifamily sales this year, although it marked a discount for the Atlanta-based seller
By Julia Echikson August 28, 2026 1:30 pm
reprintsMultifamily development firm Cortland sold a garden-style rental complex in West Palm Beach, Fla., for $208 million, property records show. The transaction ranks among South Florida’s largest multifamily sales this year, although it marked a discount for the Atlanta-based seller.
Fairfield Residential bought the 812-unit asset, called Portofino Place Apartments. The property houses 34 three-story buildings across nearly 40 acres at 4400 and 4600 Portofino Way, between North Military Trail and Interstate 95..
The deal equates to about $256,200 per apartment and occurred through two deeds. One, valued at $108 million, covered 416 units built in 2003. The other, valued at $100 million, covered the remaining 396 apartments, which were built in 2006.
The buyer nabbed just over $178 million in financing, assuming two loans, with $93.1 million and $85 million respectively in outstanding debt. Both loans, which are backed by Freddie Mac, are scheduled to mature in September 2033.
Cortland purchased the complex for a combined $229 million in 2021, during the height of the pandemic when rents skyrocketed. The nearly $20 million loss is likely in part due to rent growth having slowed since then.
The recent sale follows another big sale from Cortland. In May, it sold the 456-unit Uptown Boca Villas for $240 million to the real estate investment arm of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The deal remains South Florida’s largest multifamily sale so far this year.
Representatives for Cortland and Fairfield Residential did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.

Kevin Warsh Notes Inflation Concerns But Offers No Clues as to Next Fed Decision
The Fed chair said in Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not ‘meaningfully improved’
By Andrew Coen August 28, 2026 11:24 am
reprintsNew Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did not tip his hand Friday about whether an interest rate hike is on the horizon but did voice concerns about a continued trend of higher inflation.
“I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision,” Warsh said in prepared remarks at the central bank’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyo. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.”
Warsh, who assumed the Fed leadership post in June from Jerome Powell, stressed Friday that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remains committed to keeping its 2 percent annual inflation rate as a target. He said that recent personal consumption expenditures and the consumer price index have performed “better than expected,” but also noted that underlying inflation trends have not “meaningfully improved.”
The FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rates at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent during Warsh’s first two meetings. Warsh has sought to change the Fed’s long-standing forward-guidance policy often used by markets when interpreting the central bank’s data, a position he re-emphasized Friday.
“We determine the path of short-term interest rates, and market participants will always try to anticipate what we will do next,” Warsh said. “But we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade.”
The FOMC’s next meeting is scheduled for Sept. 15-16. Markets have priced in about a 50 percent chance of a rate hike based on Investing.com’s latest Fed rate monitor tool.
Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

Knighthead Funding Refis Chicago-Area Apartments With $32M Loan
By Andrew Coen August 28, 2026 10:58 am
reprintsThe Drake Group has sealed a $32 million loan to refinance a newly built multifamily community in suburban Chicago, Commercial Observer has learned.
Knighthead Funding supplied the loan for the 62-unit the Drake Group’s Cerca property in Glenview, Ill., that opened in June. The debt refinances a previous construction facility and pays off the property’s preferred equity investor, according to Knighthead.
“Cerca is a great addition to Glenview’s residential landscape,” Jonathan Daniel, principal of Knighthead Funding, said in a statement. “We’re pleased to provide the Drake Group with a flexible refinancing solution that supports this best-in-class property.”
Daniel originated the refi with a Knighthead team that also featured Peter Illuzzi and Joseph Marraccini.
JLL negotiated the debt with a team consisting of Daniel Gillard, Philip Galligan, Michael Gurwin and Ryan Planek.
Located at 1850 Glenview Road 19 miles north of Downtown Chicago, the property benefits from mass transit access to Glenview’s Metra station, according to Knighthead. Community amenities include a fitness center, a conference rooms, a dog spa, and grilling stations. It also includes 6,886 square feet of ground-floor retail space.
The Drake Group did not immediately return a request for comment.
Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

The move is part of Meridian’s strategy to appeal to nontraditional defense and security tenants
By Greg Cornfield August 27, 2026 6:15 pm
reprintsMeridian Group and Harrison Street Asset Management have acquired a five-building office portfolio in Chantilly, Va., as part of a broader push to attract national security, defense and intelligence firms as tenants.
The joint venture, which also includes HLM Associates, acquired the Stoneleigh and Newbrook campuses totaling 431,000 square feet in the Westfields submarket of Fairfax County. The buyers said they plan additional capital investments to expand secure-facility capabilities and to modernize infrastructure across the portfolio.
The companies did not disclose pricing. Bisnow reported the sale price at approximately $67 million, citing a source familiar with the deal. The five properties are at 4800 and 4840 Westfields Boulevard and 14150, 14151 and 14155 Newbrook Drive. An affiliate of the RMR Group sold the properties, records show.
The acquisition is the first for Meridian’s platform around secure, mission-critical facilities, according to Gary Block, the Bethesda-based firm’s chief investment officer.
“Our goal is to become a landlord of choice for both traditional government contractors and the growing universe of nontraditional defense and technology companies in the markets we serve,” Block said in a statement.
Harrison Street, which has approximately $109 billion in assets under management, said the strategy targets specialized properties benefiting from government-related demand and high barriers to entry. HLM also has expertise in the development and operation of facilities supporting classified government operations.
Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.

Stratford Partners JV Buys San Diego-Area Apartments for $34M
By Greg Cornfield August 27, 2026 5:25 pm
reprintsA joint venture between Stratford Partners and LLJ has acquired a 189-unit apartment complex in northern San Diego County.
The joint venture put down $33.6 million for Pacifica Palms Apartments at 1861 East Washington Avenue in Escondido, according to Institutional Property Advisors (IPA), a division of Marcus & Millichap. The deal works out to about $178,000 per unit.
An entity named Pacifica Palms LLC, run by David J. Snodgrass and Barbara Snodgrass, sold the property, records with PropertyShark show.
The gated Pacifica Palms includes 20 buildings across 8 acres on East Washington Avenue, about 2.5 miles from Downtown Escondido. The development was completed more than 60 years ago.
IPA’s Chris Zorbas and Alexander Garcia Jr. represented the seller and procured the buyer. Zorbas described the property as a rare chance to acquire a large value-add multifamily asset in a supply-constrained submarket.
“The Escondido submarket has seen limited availability of multifamily assets of this size,” Zorbas said in a statement.
Garcia pointed to the widening cost gap between renting and owning, as Escondido home prices have increased 19 percent since 2021, according to IPA.
“The disparity between monthly living expenses for renting versus owning should sustain low vacancy and place upward pressure on Escondido’s rental prices for the foreseeable future,” Garcia said.
San Diego’s multifamily market remains tight, with vacancy at 4.2 percent earlier this year, and average effective rents of $2,832 per month, according to Marcus & Millichap’s most recent multifamily report. Deal flow also improved by 25 percent during the 12 months ending in March. Escondido is among the tighter, more affordable submarkets, where limited vacancy is expected to persist.
Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.

Walmart has signed an industrial lease in Miami-Dade County, likely spanning more than 130,000 square feet.
The retail giant inked a deal at Seagis Property Group’s newly completed warehouse at 10900 Northwest 138th Street in Medley, facing West Okeechobee Road near the Florida Turnpike, property records show. The 16-year lease includes three five-year extensions.
Public documents suggest the tenant will occupy the entire 130,150-square-foot property, which rises 40 feet tall and includes two drive-in doors and 46 dock-high doors. A spokesperson for Walmart declined to comment. A representative for the landlord did not respond to requests for comment.
Seagis Property Group completed the warehouse this year after buying the 13.2-acre site for $17.5 million in 2022.
In another recent South Florida deal, Bentonville, Ark.-based Walmart bought a 24-acre parcel in Palm Beach County for $11.7 million in August to build a superstore. Walmart also renewed its 83,342-square-foot industrial lease at 1981 North Powerline Road in Pompano Beach late last year, according to a market report from Cushman & Wakefield.
Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.

Savills Inks 20K-SF Deal at Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue
By Emily Davis August 27, 2026 2:10 pm
reprintsThe deal-makers at Savills have struck a lease of their own.
The global real estate advisory firm is expanding its New York City presence by taking 20,481 square feet for a satellite office at Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue, according to a Thursday announcement by the landlord. Savills will occupy the entire third floor at the 22-story Midtown East tower for a five-year term.
Asking rent for the deal was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for Midtown office space was $84.88 per square foot in July, according to Colliers.
Rudin’s Kevin Daly and Craig Panzirer represented the landlord in-house in the deal, alongside a CBRE team of Brett Shannon, Peter Turchin, Eric Deutsch, Lauren Levy and Jacob Rosenthal. Savills represented itself in the transaction.
Savills’ new office space sits four blocks north of its U.S. headquarters at 399 Park Avenue.
The new lease will accommodate Savills’ program and project management group, a spokesperson for the brokerage told Commercial Observer. The added elbow room comes just a few weeks after Savills completed its acquisition and launch of Eastdil Secured Savills in a major platform expansion.
Situated at the corner of East 50th Street and Lexington Avenue three blocks east of Rockefeller Center, 560 Lexington has attracted more than 110,000 square feet of deals that have now been completed there this year, according to Rudin.
Hedge fund SummitTX Capital took nearly 18,000 square feet across the 19th floor earlier this year, Commercial Observer reported, followed by investment firm Ally Bridge Group’s 6,440-square-foot relocation in May, financial firm Marex’s 39,552-square-foot deal in April, and sports investment firm Dynasty Equity’s 9,910-square-foot lease in June.
Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

Vivmark Residential Transfers $742M California Multifamily Portfolio from Avalon
The new apartments are approximately 1,843 units within the Vivmark portfolio, which spans more than 180,000 units across the country
By Brian Pascus August 27, 2026 12:58 pm
reprintsFollowing a generational merger, the largest apartment real estate investment trust (REIT) in the business just made things a little more official.
Days after AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed their $71 billion merger — the largest merger of publicly traded REITs in history — the new firm, Vivmark Residential, has transferred seven apartment complexes in Northern California near San Francisco, totaling more than 1,800 units, at a value of $741.8 million into the new company.
The Mercury News first reported the transfer to Vivmark Residential, a public entity that now boasts a portfolio in excess of 180,000 rental apartment units.
The properties include Avalon Campbell, a 348-unit complex at 508 Railway Avenue in Campbell, Calif., valued at $147.3 million; Avalon Towers on the Peninsula, a 238-unit complex at 2400 West El Camino Real in Mountain View, Calif., valued at $140.4 million; Avalon Fremont, a 308-unit complex at 39939 Stevenson Common in Fremont, Calif., valued at $124.3 million; Eaves Creekside, a 300-unit apartment at 151 Calderon Avenue in Mountain View, Calif., valued at $117.3 million; Eaves Fremont, a 237-unit complex at 231 Woodcreek Common in Fremont valued at $88.9 million; Eaves Dublin, a 204-unit apartment at 7904 Fall Creek Road in Dublin, Calif., valued at $64.6 million; and Eaves Union City, a 208-unit complex at 2175 Decoto Road in Union City, Calif., valued at $59.1 million.
Brad Dillman, founder and principal of Florey Street Advisors, told CO after the merger was announced that both AvalonBay and Equity had “enormous coastal exposure across both firms,” and that “they overlap in like 95 percent of their geographies.”
Vivmark Residential did not respond to requests for comment by press time
Correction: This was initially reported as a sale, but it was actually a transfer of property into the new entity.
Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialosberver.com.

Construction is underway on the $36 million renovation and expansion of the Eastern Parkway Library, a two-story Classical Revival Carnegie library at 1044 Eastern Parkway in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. Designed by Allied Works and managed by the New York City Department of Design and Construction for Brooklyn Public Library, the project will expand the 12,250-square-foot branch’s public space by more than 50 percent and add a 13,400-square-foot, three-story wing along Schenectady Avenue. The project will also include a renovated courtyard with outdoor seating, a third-floor reading terrace surrounded by greenery, and a permanent home for the branch’s Adult Learning Center.
Renderings show the original structure restored to its architectural integrity, with the five-bay limestone façade, arched entrance portal, and distinctive long arched windows retained and repaired. The new wing rises behind a large glass façade and contains a double-height reading room filled with natural light, overlooked by a reading mezzanine. The interior palette consists of untreated Belgian oak, coal terrazzo, perforated metal ceilings, and precast concrete. A new ramped entrance, elevator, and restrooms will make the building fully ADA-compliant, while a green roof, high-performance glazing, and upgraded HVAC, plumbing, and fire alarm systems are expected to bring the building to LEED Silver certification.
Reconfigured interiors will contain a main reading room, a teen zone, two children’s zones, a STEAM room, a multipurpose room with a projector, a community room, and a classroom in the restored fireplace room. Through the Department of Cultural Affairs’ Percent for Art program, Brooklyn-based artist Oasa DuVerney will install a series of reflective portraits of writers from the African diaspora on the reading mezzanine.
The branch is closed for the duration of construction. A temporary pop-up library will open in the neighborhood this fall, with space provided by Settlement Housing Fund, furnishings donated by IKEA, and additional support from Amazon.

sources.retrieved_text:
The affordable housing lottery has launched for 132 Brown Place, a five-story mixed-use building at 496 East 134th Street in Port Morris, The Bronx. Designed by Boaz M. Golani Architect and developed by Lefko Capital Group, the structure yields 44 residences. Available on NYC Housing Connect are nine units for residents at 80 percent of the area median income (AMI), ranging in eligible income from $67,886 to $146,560.
Amenities include bike storage lockers, a shared laundry room, elevator, and security cameras. Tenant is responsible for electricity including heat and stove.
At 80 percent of the AMI, there are two studios with a monthly rent of $1,812 for incomes ranging from $67,886 to $108,560; two one-bedrooms with a monthly rent of $2,283 for incomes ranging from $84,858 to $122,160; and five two-bedrooms with a monthly rent of $2,713 for incomes ranging from $101,863 to $146,560.
Prospective renters must meet income and household size requirements to apply for these apartments. Applications must be postmarked or submitted online no later than August 19, 2026.Housin

candidates.title: NYC eyes new requirements for treatment of pregnant people in police custody
candidates.what_happened:
New York City Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers at a City Council hearing. 
  

 The City Council bills were introduced three months after Samantha Randazzo, then nine months pregnant, gave birth to a boy while in NYPD custody in a Brooklyn courtroom. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
New York City could impose new requirements on the NYPD's treatment of pregnant New Yorkers in custody and require police to track children who are present when their parents or caregivers are arrested.
The push comes after a high-profile incident earlier this year when a woman gave birth in a Brooklyn courtroom. The City Council bills were introduced three months after Samantha Randazzo, then nine months pregnant, gave birth to a boy while in NYPD custody after she was arrested on low-level drug and trespassing charges.
Public defenders and legal advocates have said prosecutors could have declined to prosecute the case or a judge could have dismissed it.
The city has previously settled lawsuits with other women who said they were forced to give birth while restrained by officers, including an incident in 2018 when a woman was arrested two days after her due date and went into labor in a holding cell without water.
The Queens elected official behind the newly introduced legislation said she drafted the bills “almost immediately” after she learned of this year’s incident.
“I was instantly just furious at the lack of dignity and respect that was shown to this woman and just the lack of thought from anyone having the thought that this is an emergency situation and that actions need to be taken to get her the proper medical attention,” Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers said in a statement. “At the end of the day, she’s still just a person enduring one of the most vulnerable moments in her life.”
The first bill, Intro. 995, would require the NYPD to train officers on laws, rules and policies governing the use of restraints on people in custody who are pregnant or postpartum. It would also require the department to publicly report each year on how many officers received the training.
The second bill, Intro. 996, would require the police department to report quarterly on arrests where a child was present, including the number and ages of the children and whether they were left in the care of another adult.
The legislation is backed by several organizations that advocate for currently and formerly incarcerated New Yorkers and their families, including the Bronx-based Osborne Association.
“When an individual is involved in the criminal justice system there are these ripple effects that benefit all of us to pay attention and to support children who are affected by their parents’ arrest and incarceration,” said Tanya Krupat, the organization’s vice president for policy and advocacy.
The city legislation comes after state lawmakers passed a bill that would restrict the use of restraints on people in police custody who are pregnant, in labor or delivery or within 12 weeks after a pregnancy ends, with limited exceptions.
That bill, which was originally introduced in January 2025, swiftly passed the state Senate and Assembly weeks after Randazzo gave birth in May. The legislation is awaiting Gov. Kathy Hochul's signature.
“We are reviewing the legislation. The Mamdani administration is committed to delivering a criminal justice system that safeguards the health and well-being of all New Yorkers, including those who are pregnant and post partum," Sam Raskin, Mayor Mamdani's Deputy Press Secretary, said in a statement. "We also are dedicated to ensuring that all city agencies take appropriate transparency measures.”

Office Leads Pricing Gains as RCA CPPI Inches Up in July 2026
U.S. commercial property prices edged higher in July as the RCA CPPI US National All-Property Index posted its slowest annual gain since January 2025, MSCI Real Assets reported. The index increased 0.2% from a year earlier and rose 0.1% from June, translating to an annualized growth pace of 1.2%.
“Borrowing costs for commercial real estate show no sign of easing, as the Federal Reserve held its policy rate steady in a divided vote and its chair ruled out any softening of the inflation target,” reported MSCI. “Investors now see scant chance of a near-term rate cut, keeping financing conditions tight across the market.”
By property type, CBD office was the best performer, with prices up 9.9% from a year ago and 1.6% from June. Suburban office pricing also increased, up 4.0% annually and 0.4% from the previous month. The other major property sectors experienced annual declines, ranging from 0.9% for retail to 4.4% for apartments. July marked the ninth consecutive month of annual declines for apartment pricing.

The release of a citywide strategy for building 2,100 public bathrooms will be delayed after Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s team said the task is too complicated to meet its deadline.
The legislation, dubbed the Bathroom Bill, passed the City Council in April 2025 and set out to create a comprehensive plan to double the number of public restrooms by 2035. Each relevant agency was supposed to file an updated strategic plan to maintain the network of loos by Sept. 1, with updates every four years.
But Deputy Mayor Julia Kerson sent a letter on Aug. 12 to Speaker Julie Menin saying they’re backed up.
“Given the extensive cross-agency coordination required to establish a reporting framework, compile baseline data, and develop a substantive strategy toward the law’s target of 2,120 public bathrooms citywide, I am writing to inform you that the report will be submitted after the September 1 deadline,” she wrote.
MORE: Prefab Potty Hyped as Fast and Cheap Is Years Late, Will Cost NYC $3.5M
The mayor’s team has, however, started work on the ambitious plan — including “an interagency working group” and site recommendations.
City Hall hopes to submit the report by Nov. 1, Kerson wrote.
City Councilmember Sandy Nurse (D-Brooklyn) introduced the package of bills last year to find easier, cheaper ways to add more quality bathrooms across the city — and was looking forward to the upcoming report.
There are currently 1,066 public bathrooms in the city, and 943 are open year-round, Nurse said.
“People don’t realize there’s no particular agency or mayoral office tasked with bathrooms,” she told The City Reporter. She and some other councilmembers representing Brooklyn were briefed this month by City Hall on some of the newest bathrooms for their borough.
MORE: Mamdani Pitches New Public Toilets While 50 Park Bathrooms Sit Closed
Nurse said she hopes the report can identify inventive and inexpensive ways to add more public bathrooms.
“What are the new models coming out? What are places across the country, across the planet, what are they doing?” she said. “What are we doing to decrease the cost and cut down on red tape?”
Mamdani in January announced a request for proposals to build modular public bathrooms across the city. In June, the administration announced it had selected Throne Labs Inc. to install and maintain 17 modular public bathrooms. The $4 million pilot program will be overseen by the city’s Economic Development Corp.
“My administration is committed to closing the gaps in this public health infrastructure,” Mamdani said in a statement at the time, “and delivering a network of restrooms that are clean, accessible, and most importantly, close by.”

candidates.what_happened:

sources.retrieved_text:
The city’s Department of Correction has blown past a new deadline to give Rikers Island detainees a digital platform to review evidence in their cases.
The access was mandated by the City Council last year which gave DOC nine months — until July 1 — to find a vendor and implement the evidence review system through tablets or another secure platform.
The legislation could have a game-changing impact for detainees at the scandal-scarred jail complex who are fighting criminal cases. About 85% of the nearly 6,500 people held on Rikers Island are awaiting trial and have not been convicted of a crime.
There’s no timeline in place to meet the new legal requirement. A jail source told The City Reporter that security concerns had slowed the project.
“It’s been a long time coming, but they just haven’t got it done yet,” said Zachary Katznelson, executive director of the Independent Rikers Commission, which advocates for the closure of the jail complex and wrote a report advocating for digital access.
The DOC has been working on it for at least two years and is in talks with a tech company called Lighting Law which provides similar evidence-access technology to other lockups around the country, according to multiple jail insiders.
In those locations, each detainee receives an individual account that they can use on their department issued tablet and via computers in law libraries. Their defense lawyers can upload the evidence — including large videos — onto the site.
The delayed implementation comes as a court-appointed remediation manager has ordered top jail officials to come up with a series of other reform plans over the next year after more than a decade of failed similar attempts led by Steve Martin, a federal monitor based in Texas.
MORE: ‘Bedlam’ as Rikers Island Can’t Keep Its Doors Locked
As for the evidence initiative, at stake is the ability for Rikers detainees to fully participate in their defense. Currently, Department Correction officials cannot provide detainees with an easy way to review electronic evidence.
“So to watch videotapes, to listen to phone calls, any of that is incredibly difficult, and sometimes virtually impossible,” Katznelson told The City Reporter. “And that means that people can’t prepare properly for their trials.”
Detainees can receive discovery materials by snail mail or review them by using drives accessible on law library computers located in each jail facility. They can also talk about the case with their lawyers by phone, video conference, or during in-person visits.
But they often struggle to get all the information they need to make informed decisions in court, according to criminal defense lawyers and jail reformers.
“Right now, people in custody face enormous barriers to defending themselves,” City Councilmember Jennifer Gutiérrez (D-Brooklyn), the lead sponsor of the bill, said last September as the bill passed in the Council.
“It is much harder, if not impossible, to meaningfully participate in your own defense simply due to a lack of access,” she added. “Technology has transformed nearly every part of our lives, including our courts and justice system, so it must transform in our jails as well.”
Patrick Rocchio, a DOC spokesperson, said the department is “actively working to finalize a contract for the required technology.”
“And we expect to have more to share on this soon,” he added.
Rocchio declined to detail who at the department was leading the negotiations and why it had dragged on so long.
A jail source familiar with the talks said the department has been worried about potential security lapses in which detainees are granted access to materials they’re not cleared to view. One hypothetical example involved a defendant facing child abuse charges receiving a video of the alleged misconduct. Only defense lawyers should have access to those manner of videos; they are not cleared to be shared online via the Lighting Law site.
MORE: Rikers Remediation Manager Unveils Blueprint for Overhauling City Jails
Lighting Law is already in place in approximately 15 other jails throughout the country.
But none are as large as Rikers.
The tech firm was started by Alisa Brodkowitz, an attorney who represents the families of plane crash victims. She got the idea to create an online access system as she struggled to share information with family members in Ethiopia and Kenya with loved ones who died in a crash of the Boeing 737 Max.
The new Council law did not include any penalty for a failure to implement the initiative.
But the ongoing delay could open the department to a potential class action lawsuit by detainees seeking better access to evidence.
The DOC has blown past several other legally mandated deadlines.
The department was obligated to issue a report by May 1 updating the public on its broad plan to close Rikers. The DOC also had recent deadlines for a report detailing ways it plans to reform the department, as well as one explaining how it uses powers to let some people serving a year or less out early.
“These are answers that New Yorkers are hungry for,” Katznelson said. “How are we going to have a system that actually keeps people safe? How are we going to have a system that actually is effective at improving public safety instead of hurting it?”

candidates.what_happened: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh vowed to curb inflation during a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

sources.retrieved_text:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh offered a sanguine economic outlook in a closely watched speech Friday that left room for future interest rate hikes as the central bank works to tame inflation.
“Credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint,” Warsh told the audience in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Friday morning. “Certain sectors like housing and agriculture are showing strains, but on balance, I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.”
In his first major speech at the top of the central bank, Warsh also offered his views on the impact of artificial intelligence on the economy and an argument against the forward guidance that has been part of Fed communications since the Global Financial Crisis.
The speech solidified Warsh’s position as an inflation hawk, as the chairman promised again to deliver price stability. For commercial real estate owners and investors, it is the latest and clearest signal that the Fed isn’t inching toward rate relief.
Warsh said the central bank had done a good job on the employment side of its dual mandate but still had work to do to bring inflation down to the Fed’s longtime 2% target rate.
The U.S. lost 23,000 jobs in July, well off economists' forecasts of roughly 83,000 new jobs, but the unemployment rate ticked down slightly to 4.1%. Job growth has been uneven in the last two years, with job losses in seven of the last 20 months, according to an NBC News analysis.
Warsh said that labor markets always have areas of concern, with recent graduates facing hurdles today, but the current market remains robust.
“They may well be concerned about future labor disruptions,” he said. “But as of now, I believe the labor markets are broadly consistent with full employment.”
Warsh, 56, outlined the principles guiding his policymaking inside the Fed, including a view that short-term interest rates are the central bank’s “predominant tool” to achieving its dual mandate.
He complained that “yesterday’s news has a way of getting mistaken for what's happening right now,” and he pledged to lead a central bank that was quieter and more purposeful in its communications.
The comments were in line with criticisms Warsh, who worked at the Fed during the GFC, had leveled against the central bank under then-Chair Jerome Powell. Warsh previously called for structural reforms inside the central bank, and he launched five task forces after he took over that are reviewing practically every aspect of Fed operations.
Warsh has been critical of the forward guidance offered after each Federal Open Market Committee meeting, arguing that the central bank risked tipping investor decision-making by telegraphing its moves ahead of time and before financial conditions supported them.
“We should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade,” Warsh said Friday. “If markets rely materially on the Fed's guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we're more likely to be blinded to new developments.”
On price stability, the other side of the Fed’s dual mandate, Warsh conceded that “the numbers are more concerning,” but he reiterated that he was committed to pulling inflation down.
“Inflation is running above our 2% target, so the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices,” he said.
He described the economy as at a “hinge point in history” as artificial intelligence redefines the typical roads to economic growth. The technology remains nascent, and a host of unanswered questions will define how AI broadly remakes the economy, he said.
Warsh raised questions about whether AI’s adoption would result in a significant and sustained boost to productivity, how much competition would exist between leading AI models, and where capital would settle between materials providers, chipmakers, AI-model operators, energy producers and cloud infrastructure providers.
The chairman said businesses were rapidly increasing their capital expenditures while profit margins were at historical highs. Investors are looking for growth in both earnings and outside investment, and credit spreads on corporate bond issuance remain strong.
“I'm impressed by the overall performance of the economy, which appears to have strengthened,” Warsh said.

If you need a new refrigerator condenser or thermostat, Parts Town Unlimited will have you covered from Pendergrass, Georgia.
The parts supplier focused on food service, appliances and HVAC original equipment manufacturer parts has leased 538,400 SF at Building 1 of Jackson 85 North Business Park, some 100 miles north of Downtown Atlanta, according to a press release.
Jackson 85 North will serve as Parts Town’s largest global fulfillment center behind its facilities in Chicago, Phoenix and Munich and will support more than 140 local jobs, according to the release. The new facility can deliver parts to more than 90% of the U.S. within two days.
“By placing greater depth and breadth of mission-critical OEM parts closer to customers across the Southeast, we can reduce transit times and costs,” Parts Town CEO Bill Geary said in the release.
The lease covers the entire building, which is owned and developed by Trammell Crow Co. and CBRE Investment Management. Wilson Hull Neal’s Bilijack Bell, Joseph Rogers, Conner Dickinson and Will Geraghty represented the landlords, while SK Commercial Realty brokered for the tenant.
Jackson 85 North still has a second 1M SF speculative Class-A warehouse on its 215 acres as part of the first phase of its development, according to the release.
LEASES
Gym chain EōS Fitness inked a long-term 38K SF lease for a new location at 965 North Point Drive in Alpharetta, part of the North Point Commons shopping center. The gym is taking over a space previously occupied by the defunct arts and crafts retailer Joann Fabric and Crafts.
Joann shuttered all its Georgia locations under bankruptcy last year.
The landlord, Realty Income, represented itself, while SRS Real Estate Partners represented the tenant.
ASSIGNMENTS
Evergreen Medical Properties has tapped Transwestern’s John Lopez and Bo Stuart to lease up Northside Alpharetta Medical Campus, a four-building, 415K SF medical office property at 3400 Old Milton Parkway in North Fulton County. More than 200 medical tenants within the Northside Hospital network are tenants in the property.
***
Selig Enterprises Inc. has tapped Partners Real Estate’s John Zintak, Will Porter and Gracie Swan to lease the remaining 30K SF of space available at the firm’s 1105 West Peachtree, a 675K SF trophy office tower in Midtown that is home to Google and law firm Smith Gambrell & Russell.
The tower is part of a larger mixed-use project that includes luxury condominium tower 40 West 12th and the Epicurean Atlanta hotel.
Beyond the office building, the trio is also helping Selig lure potential tenants that could kick off new developments at the firm’s Midtown land holdings, including 1125 Peachtree St., 48 12th St. and 1200 Spring St., the Atlanta Business Chronicle reported.
DEVELOPMENT
Thompson Thrift has broken ground on Avira at Silver Comet Trail, a 319-unit apartment complex in Powder Springs that is expected to deliver by October of next year. Located at the corner of Georgia Highway 278 and Isley Stamper Road, the site is adjacent to the more than 60-mile Silver Comet pedestrian trail, which runs from Smyrna to the border of Alabama.
Amenities will include a resort-style swimming pool, fitness center, pickleball court, dog park and pet spa, as well as coworking suites, grilling areas and other lifestyle-focused amenities, according to a release. Thompson Thrift capitalized the project with equity from its Thompson Thrift 2026 Multifamily Development fund.
***
The world’s largest retailer, Walmart, plans to develop a high-tech fulfillment center in Carnesville, creating 1,000 new jobs and investing $1.3B in the Franklin County community, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced this week.
Walmart plans to develop a 1.5M SF automated facility at the Franklin 85 Logistics Center, designed to help the retailer fulfill same-day and next-day shipping across the U.S.
The Georgia Department of Economic Development's Elizabeth McLean represented the state in incentive negotiations with Walmart.
SALES
Dallas-based S2 Capital sold The Bowie, a 350-unit, garden-style apartment complex at 8800 Dunwoody Place in Sandy Springs, to an undisclosed buyer for an undisclosed price, according to a Newmark press release.
The nearly 30-acre property in Central Perimeter is 86% leased. Newmark’s Brooks Colquitt, James Wilber, David Gutting, Derrick Bloom and Hunter Amos brokered the sale. Fulton County property records did not reflect a sale as of press time.
S2 purchased the complex in 2022 for $68M, according to Fulton County property records. The firm obtained a $54.5M loan from Acore Capital at the time, which was set to mature in December 2027.
Fulton County valued the property at $27.6M earlier this year, a nearly 60% discount to S2’s purchase price.
Sherman Residential purchased Celadon on Club, a 352-unit apartment complex in Lawrenceville, from an LLC attached to Atlanta-based Oxford Properties for an undisclosed sum. The Class-A, garden-style apartments off Club Drive were developed in 2023.
Gwinnett County did not reflect a current sales transaction, but the county valued the property at $55M earlier this year.
***
Minnesota-based The Terrace Group paid $12.65M for Columbia Colony Senior Residences, a 62-year-old apartment community at 2999 Continental Road in Atlanta, from Utah-based Columbia Colony Whitaker LLC, according to sales tax records in the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database.
According to Fulton County property records, the LLC is tied to Peak Capital Partners, which paid $9.2M in 2019 for the 120-unit property.
***
1325 Virginia Hospitality LLC purchased the Sonesta Atlanta Airport North, a 378-room hotel off Virginia Avenue near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, from an LLC tied to Tremont Realty Capital in Massachusetts, according to sales tax records in the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database.
The local LLC, which is tied to the Lawrenceville law firm Mills Walls Alioto, is connected to a $10M project that recently underwent a room refresh, according to JLL, which previously marketed the property for sale, according to an internet archive of the website.

sources.retrieved_text:
$36M renovation of historic Eastern Parkway Library breaks ground
All images courtesy of NYC Mayor’s Office unless noted otherwise
Work has begun on the $36 million transformation of Crown Heights’ historic Eastern Parkway Library. Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday announced the start of the project, which will expand public space at the century-old Brooklyn Public Library branch at 1044 Eastern Parkway by more than 50 percent while preserving its historic architecture. Led by the city’s Department of Design and Construction, the project is expected to be completed in summer 2028.
Established in 1914, the original two-story library was designed by Raymond F. Almirall and built as part of a $5.2 million gift from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie to establish a comprehensive library system across New York City.
The Classical Revival-style building features a limestone facade and long, arched windows. Inside, double-height reading rooms offer ample natural light, with mezzanines overlooking the lower level.
Designed by Allied Works, the renovation will expand the library’s public space by 12,250 square feet and add a 13,400-square-foot, three-story wing along Schenectady Avenue, according to Yimby.
Renderings detail a material palette of untreated Belgian oak, coal terrazzo, perforated metal ceilings, and precast concrete that pays homage to the original architecture, according to e-architect.
A new, expansive glass facade will bring even more natural light into the library and make the building fully ADA-compliant, with a new elevator and entrance ramp.
The facility will also feature dedicated reading and learning spaces, including a multipurpose room with a projector, a main reading room, a teen zone, two children’s zones, a STEAM room, a community room, and a classroom in the building’s restored fireplace room.
The renovation will also add modern, energy-efficient lighting and upgrade the library’s plumbing, HVAC, and fire alarm systems. After the renovation, the library is expected to achieve LEED Silver certification.
Artwork by local artist Oasa DuVerney will also be displayed throughout the library through the Department of Cultural Affairs’ Percent for Art Program.
During construction, library services will continue at a temporary location provided by the Settlement Housing Fund, with furniture donated by IKEA and additional support for interim services provided by Amazon. When the temporary branch opens this fall, patrons will be able to check out books, attend programs, and use technology.
“The Eastern Parkway Library has served Brooklyn for over a century. The renovation—which will bring more natural light into the branch, add modern technology and create inspiring spaces—will ensure that Eastern Parkway Library can serve the community for another 100 years,” Linda E. Johnson, President and CEO of BPL, said.
The project is funded by the Office of the Mayor, the City Council, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, and the state Assembly.
The Eastern Parkway Library’s transformation is the first of three projects that Allied Works is undertaking with the DDC. The others are EMS Station 17 in the Bronx and the Jackson Heights Library. The firm received a 2020 Excellence in Design Award from the city’s Public Design Commission, according to e-architect.
“Libraries are the beating heart of civic spaces in New York, providing essential spaces and services to every community,” Brad Cloepfil, principal and founder of Allied Works, said, as reported by e-architect.
“Our redesign of the Eastern Parkway Library honors the 112-year-old building and the people it serves, paying homage to the original Carnegie library building, while expanding its public spaces.”

Tuscaloosa, Ala. — Chicago-based JLL Income Property Trust has acquired Midtown Village, a 345,000-square-foot shopping center located near the University of Alabama campus in Tuscaloosa, for $94 million. The seller requested anonymity.
Built in 2007, Midtown Village consists of eight single-story buildings across a 30-acre site.
The open-air center features a mix of retailers such as Barnes & Noble, Ulta Beauty, Old Navy, Best Buy, lululemon, American Eagle & Aerie, Fab’rik, Kay Jewelers, South Boutique, Loft, Tuscaloosa Nail & Spa and GameStop. Restaurants include Panera Bread, Blaze Pizza, Metro Diner and Tropical Smoothie Café.
The tenant roster has a weighted average lease-term (WALT) of more than 16 years.
“The enduring demand of this strong tenant roster supports stable operating performance, and the center is well-positioned in a thriving submarket with proven traffic,” says Allan Swaringen, president and CEO of JLL Income Property Trust.
Midtown Village is situated on the southwest corner of McFarland Boulevard East and 15th Street and is one of the most visited retail shopping centers in the state, with over 5.7 million annual visits, according to JLL Income Property Trust. It is also located within one mile from DCH Regional Medical Center, Tuscaloosa’s largest regional hospital.
With the addition of this investment, grocery-anchored and necessity-driven retail investments comprise 13 percent of JLL Income Property Trust’s $7 billion portfolio. The company now owns 22 open-air shopping centers with a value of approximately $900 million.
— Abby Cox

An official website of the United States government
News Release 2026-72 | August 27, 2026
Share This Page:
OCC issues two revised policies and procedures manuals; proposes amendments to Violations of Laws and Regulations framework
WASHINGTONâThe Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced additional actions to focus supervisory attention on the most significant risks and violations and to provide banks greater clarity, consistency and certainty in how Matters Requiring Attention (MRA) and enforcement actions are issued.
In connection with the final rule regarding unsafe or unsound practices and MRAs issued jointly today with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the OCC has substantially revised its policies and procedures manuals (PPMs) regarding enforcement actions and MRAs.
âToday, the OCC is taking a number of historic steps to codify the agencyâs return to risk-based supervision, helping to ensure that its more reasonable, intentional approach to bank supervision endures,â said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould. âIt is critical that examiners and institutions prioritize material financial risks and substantive violations of law over concerns related to policies, process, documentation, and other nonfinancial risks, and that the agenciesâ supervision and enforcement standards further that prioritization.â
Revisions to PPM 5310-3, âBank Enforcement Action and Related Matters,â emphasize material financial risks, and highlight OCCâs three guiding principles when considering bank enforcement actionsâescalation, tailoring, and focusing corrective actions on those essential to address specific deficiencies.
In addition to focusing banksâ and examinersâ attention on issues that materially affect safety, soundness, and compliance with laws and regulations, these revisions also ensure enforcement tools are used proportionately and predictably. Under the revision, the OCC may escalate to an enforcement action against a large or complex bank based on practices that would not trigger a similar response against a community bank â reflecting the increased regulatory and supervisory expectations for large or complex banks in the revised enforcement approach.
Additionally, the OCC is releasing PPM 5400-11, âMatters Requiring Attention,â publicly for the first time to provide greater clarity and transparency regarding its supervisory standards.
Revisions to this PPM reflect the supervisory framework in the joint final rule and clarify the OCC will only issue an MRA for practices, acts, or failures to act that meet the listed standard. The PPM also directs that MRAs must be tailored based on financial risk-related factors.
Along with the revised PPMs, the OCC released for public comment a notice of proposed rulemaking to codify its supervisory framework for the issuance of MRAs in response to violations of laws or regulations.
The proposed rule would establish and define two categories of violations of laws or regulations: âsubstantive violationsâ and âtechnical violations.â The proposed distinction intends to focus supervisory attention on violations that have the greatest impact on an institution or its customers. For those not substantive in nature, the proposed rule would provide a mechanism to address the violations outside of an MRA.
The OCC remains committed to addressing the challenges for its regulated institutions of all sizes and has taken a series of actions to rightsize regulatory burden and tailor supervisory activities to deliver the Administrationâs vision of Parallel Prosperity for Main Street and Wall Street. candidates.title: New Jersey governor signs law requiring data centers to report energy and water use
candidates.what_happened: Follows new rate class establishment in July

facts.name: amount
facts.evidence_span: w disclosure laws, Sherrill also signed a law that ends the $500 million tax credit program that encouraged the development of new d

sources.retrieved_text:
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill has signed into law new rules requiring data center owners and operators in New Jersey to disclose their energy and water use to state regulators.
The new laws will require data centers to submit semiannual reports to the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities detailing total energy consumption, energy used for cooling versus IT equipment, peak daily water use, water sources, and on-site and backup power supplies.
The new law follows legislation signed by the governor in July that mandated data center firms bring their own clean energy and established a new utility rate class for large-load data centers to mitigate cost shifting to regular ratepayers. The rules apply to both existing and new facilities with a capacity exceeding 100MW.
"At the beginning of this summer, I announced the most comprehensive data center plan in the nation to establish strong guardrails and hold data centers accountable," said Sherrill. "Just three months later, I am delivering on all four pillars of that plan."
Environmental groups said that the new laws do not go far enough, with several calling for a statewide moratorium on new data center builds, like its neighbor New York, which became the first state to impose a statewide moratorium last month.
“Data center reporting for energy and water use after the damage is done is the antithesis of guardrails,” said Jaclyn Rhoads, executive director of the Pinelands Alliance. “New Jersey is paving the way for data centers to contaminate our air and waterways while leaving the public to suffer. We demand more of our government officials. Pass a moratorium now.”
Sherrill pushed back against these arguments, contending that data centers seeking to build in New Jersey will “play by our rules.”
“We don’t have to choose between innovation and accountability, and we won’t,” she said.
In addition to the new disclosure laws, Sherrill also signed a law that ends the $500 million tax credit program that encouraged the development of new data centers.
According to Data Center Map, New Jersey currently hosts 66 data centers across 48 operators. The market is dominated by colo providers, with Equinix, QTS, Digital Realty, and Iron Mountain, all with facilities in the state.

candidates.title: Digital Realty breaks ground on fourth data center in Zurich, Switzerland
candidates.what_happened: Company adding 15MW of capacity

sources.retrieved_text:
Digital Realty has broken ground on a new data center in Zurich, Switzerland.
The colo giant this week announced the start of construction on a new data center in Glattbrugg.
The facility – ZUR4 – will provide 15MW of IT capacity across approximately 6,300 sqm (67,810 sq ft) of space. It is due to go live in 2028.
Announced in 2023, the new data center will expand Digital’s existing campus, which hosts ZUR1, ZUR2, and ZUR3.
Digital said ZUR4 will support high-density deployments and AI workloads via “state-of-the-art” cooling systems.
Yves Zischek, managing director of Digital Realty in Austria and Switzerland, said: “With ZUR4 and the continued expansion of our campus in Glattbrugg, we are creating a future-proof ecosystem that connects more than 200 customers on-site and more than 6,000 customers worldwide.”
Digital’s three live Swiss data centers total around 25,000 sqm (269,100 sq ft) of colocation space and some 45MW of capacity. In operation since 2000 and upgraded several times, ZUR1 offers 5MW across 7,400 sqm (79,800 sq ft). Construction on ZUR2 began in 2019 and launched around 2020.
Digital (via Interxion) announced plans for ZUR3 in 2020; the first of three phases was set to launch in mid-2022 and offer 2,900 sqm (31,215 sq ft) of space. Now live, at full build-out, ZUR3 will span 11,000 sqm (118,500 sq ft) and 24MW of capacity.
“The expansion of ZUR4 vividly demonstrates how much digital infrastructure has become the backbone of the Canton of Zurich's economy. Investments like this not only secure jobs and innovative capacity, but also strengthen our digital self-determination as a location,” added Barbara Franzen, member of the Cantonal Council, FDP, Canton of Zurich.

candidates.title: T1 Energy secures approval to convert solar manufacturing campus in Mo i Rana, Norway, into 50MW data center
candidates.what_happened: With an option to expand

sources.retrieved_text:
US solar manufacturing firm T1 Energy is pivoting into the data center sector.
The company received approval from local authorities to convert a portion of its Giga Arctic solar manufacturing campus in Mo i Rana, Norway, into a data center.
The Mo i Rana municipal government approved a permit on Thursday to rezone 161,000 sq ft (15,000 sqm) of the Giga Arctic site for industrial use or data center operations. The remainder of the 926,000 sq ft (86,028 sqm) site will remain zoned for industrial development, subject to change once more grid capacity is allocated.
The data center is slated to have a capacity of 50MW and could be operational as early as next year, with the potential to expand. T1 said it holds a position in the local grid capacity queue for 396MW of capacity and believes the existing building at the site will have enough space to accommodate a data center of that size.
The company has a 50-year lease at the Giga Arctic site, with the option to extend. The site sits within an industrial park in northern Norway and, according to the company, has access to low-cost energy from the region's hydropower assets.
T1 said it is now in discussions with potential clients about monetizing the site, which was originally constructed as a solar and battery energy storage manufacturing facility.
“The people of Mo i Rana, Norway, today took a step towards the future and showed leadership in a future of AI and technology abundance with the approval of T1 Energy’s plan to convert Giga Arctic into a world-class data center. We are in active discussions with multiple counterparties to find a strategy to unlock shareholder value,” said Dan Barcelo, T1 Energy’s chairman and CEO.
T1 was formerly known as Freyr Battery. It changed its name to T1 Energy in 2025, shifting its focus from the construction of battery factories to the development of domestic US solar manufacturing. The Giga Arctic site was first announced in 2022, when the company operated under the Freyr name, but following the pivot, the company dropped plans for a battery factory. The data center would be the company’s first.

Nomad Power Solutions has announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Electricity has authorised the advancement of an energy storage demonstration project in Vermont.
Announced 26 August, the DOE authorised Nomad Power Solutions through its subsidiary Nomad Transportable Power Systems to advance into phase 3 of the Vermont Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) Demonstration Project.
The approximately US$19 million project is expected to deploy up to eight Nomad transportable battery energy storage system (BESS) units across five sites within utility Green Mountain Power’s (GMP) service territory in Vermont.
In 2023, Nomad first won a US$9.5 million DOE grant to deploy its mobile BESS in rural Vermont communities.

The DOE LDES Demonstration Grant Programme was launched in 2020, with Nomad and one other recipient being the first companies to receive grants under it. Corvias Military Living has received a US$9.5 million award to demonstrate one of the first EV-inclusive microgrids at Fort Riley in Kansas, in a project involving General Motors Defense and other GM businesses, though fewer details were provided on that project.
The project’s advancement follows GMP’s operational use of an existing Nomad system for peak management and to maintain service to customers during planned utility maintenance.
The DOE project authorisation to proceed into phase 3 moves the Vermont project into installation, integration and construction.
Nomad’s patented platform is designed to be moved among locations and used for peak management, emergency response, maintenance support, renewable energy integration and other grid-resilience applications. The project is supported by a US$9.5 million DOE award and an approximately 50% non-federal cost share, with future reimbursements subject to the terms and milestones of the cooperative agreement.
Unlike conventional stationary BESS, which are generally designed for a specific location and application, Nomad’s patented transportable platform is engineered to be redeployed as operational requirements change.
Phase 3 of the Vermont project will incorporate Nomad’s latest platform, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and microgrid-enabled controls. The project is intended to demonstrate how transportable LDES can provide a resource for improving grid reliability and resilience in rural communities.
With authorisation to proceed into phase 3, Nomad will continue work under DOE award DE-OE0000952 in accordance with the project’s Statement of Project Objectives. The milestone advances Nomad’s efforts to demonstrate transportable BESS as a resource for utilities and other critical power users whilst supporting the company’s broader commercialisation strategy across North America.
Nomad’s background and battle for commercial traction under new owner
Following its planned takeover by solar PV manufacturer T1 Energy (formerly Freyr), BESS manufacturer and system integrator Kore Power announced it would sell its subsidiary Nomad Transportable Power Systems.
On 11 June, Lixte Biotechnology Holdings, a pharmaceutical company, announced that it had entered a definitive agreement to purchase all of the outstanding equity of Nomad.
Since that time, Nomad has begun trading under the Nasdaq symbol NMAD, announced a third-generation of its Voyager mobile BESS series, has had two customer-owned BESS placed into operation by DSO Electric Cooperative in Kansas, achieved UL 9540 certification for its 1MW/2MW Traveler BESS, which was delivered to Missanabie Cree First Nation in Northern Ontario, and filed its 2026 Q2 Form 10-Q.
According to the Form 10-Q, “For the six months ended 30 June 2026, the Company incurred a net loss of US$4.3 million and used cash in operations of US$3.4 million. As of 30 June 2026, the Company had cash of $US12.6 million available to fund its operations. The Company has not generated recurring revenues since inception and has incurred negative operating cash flows as it advances its development programmes.”
Further, “The Company has not yet commenced any revenue-generating operations, does not have positive cash flows from operations, relies on stock-based compensation for a substantial portion of employee and consultant compensation, and is dependent on periodic infusions of equity capital to fund its operating requirements.”
Currently, the company’s stock price is hovering at approximately US$4. Its highest recorded price was approximately US$71 in summer 2020, falling substantially that winter.
The Form 10-Q further stated, “As a result of the foregoing, management has concluded that there is substantial doubt regarding the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern for a period of at least 12 months beyond the date these condensed consolidated financial statements are issued.”
Battery Asset Management Summit USA 2026 will be held 15-16 September in Garden Grove, California, hosted by Energy-Storage.news publisher Solar Media (part of the Informa Group). The agenda emphasises addressing the roles of AI, cybersecurity, and second-life applications, broken down into two tracks: Technical Asset Management and Commercial Asset Management. This year, the conference is also co-located with Solar & Storage Finance Summit USA. Visit the official site for more details.

sources.retrieved_text:
The Hydrogen Stream: Africa’s first PV-driven hydrogen hub powers up
Cmb-Tech has started operations at a green hydrogen facility in Walvis Bay featuring 5 MW of off-grid solar, a 5 MW proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer and 5.9 MWh of battery energy storage. The project, developed with Namibia’s Ohlthaver & List Group, has around 7,000 solar modules installed across 6.5 hectares. The developers describe it as Africa’s first fully integrated green hydrogen facility. Hydrogen produced at the site will be used in dual-fuel trucks and generators, with railway and maritime applications also planned. CMB.TECH is an initial offtaker and plans to test a hydrogen-powered freight locomotive. Siemens supplied the facility’s integrated electrical, automation and safety systems. The site also includes a hydrogen refueling station and a training center. Cmb.Tech said it plans to scale the project first to 250 MW and later to 500 MW, with potential future production of green ammonia for maritime applications. The facility adds to Namibia’s emerging hydrogen sector. HyIron’s Oshivela project began producing green hydrogen in March 2025 using a 12 MW electrolyzer powered by a 25 MW solar plant.
Tohoku University researchers have used iron oxide in a photocatalytic reaction to split water using light energy. The Japanese researchers found that photocatalytic water splitting occurs when iron oxide doped with about 1% titanium is combined with rhodium-doped strontium titanate, a hydrogen-generating photocatalyst. Electrochemical measurements showed that titanium doping reduces electrical resistance and improves n-type semiconductor properties, promoting the separation of photogenerated electrons and holes and enabling water-splitting activity.
Researchers at the University of Nottingham have investigated the microscopic structure of metal swarf from manufacturing processes as a potential substrate for hydrogen-production catalysts. Using advanced imaging, the UK researchers found nanoscale grooves and ridges on waste stainless steel, titanium and nickel alloys that can act as anchoring sites for precious metals. The team deposited small amounts of platinum onto the waste metal to produce electrocatalysts capable of splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Researchers at Durham University have found that suitable depleted North Sea fields could provide 3,659 TWh of hydrogen storage capacity, equivalent to more than seven years of projected UK electricity demand in 2040. The researchers said using the fields for hydrogen storage could also enable conventional gas-fired power plants to be phased out of the UK electricity system by 2040. Current UK hydrogen storage plans focus on salt caverns and do not include depleted fields.
Researchers at Seoul National University of Science and Technology (Seoultech) have developed an AI-based system that increased the hydrogen production efficiency of a solid oxide electrolysis cell system by 14% while reducing internal temperature spikes by 80%. The researchers said the approach uses machine learning to identify the most informative simulations, reducing the computational resources required to determine promising operating conditions while limiting thermal stresses that can affect equipment lifetime.
China has instructed its oil and gas industry to develop large-scale green hydrogen production projects, as well as hydrogen pipeline and storage infrastructure, under a new national five-year plan. The policy calls for hydrogen and its derivatives to be integrated with the country’s existing oil and gas infrastructure, including its extensive pipeline network. The plan does not specify quantitative targets, with implementation expected to depend on hydrogen market development and cooperation with local governments.

candidates.title: Trump Targets Foreign Grid Equipment as Data Centers Expand
candidates.what_happened: Trump’s order targets foreign grid equipment as utilities and data center developers contend with tight supplies and long lead times.

sources.retrieved_text:
Trump Targets Foreign Grid Equipment as Data Centers Expand
Trump’s order targets foreign grid equipment as utilities and data center developers contend with tight supplies and long lead times.
President Donald Trump has declared a national emergency over the US bulk-power system, directing the Energy Department to restrict certain foreign-produced grid equipment and impose conditions on equipment already in service.
For data center operators racing to secure power for new AI infrastructure, the order could add another constraint to equipment needed to connect projects to the grid. Transformers, inverters, controls and other bulk-power equipment already face extended lead times and sourcing risks. New federal restrictions could put additional pressure on procurement, project costs and the schedule for bringing new capacity online.
The order comes as utilities and data center developers work to expand generation and transmission infrastructure for large new loads. Its impact will depend largely on how DOE defines covered equipment, suppliers and transactions in rules expected within 120 days.
Trump’s Aug. 26 executive order generally prohibits certain foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment, including associated critical software and digital capabilities, from being purchased or installed in the US when they pose specified national-security risks. The order focuses on risks including sabotage, unauthorized access and disruption of critical infrastructure. It does not apply to facilities used for local electric distribution.
The White House said the rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence and defense production has increased US dependence on certain foreign components needed to provide abundant, reliable electricity. Continued reliance on foreign sources of bulk-power equipment creates a supply-chain vulnerability, the administration said.
The order also applies to equipment already in operation.
DOE can impose conditions on the continued use and operation of covered equipment. The Energy secretary must consider reliability, safety, replacement availability and continuity of service when imposing those conditions.
That could make equipment origin, vendor control, software, remote access and other lifecycle dependencies part of a reliability determination rather than simply a procurement decision, said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group.
“The biggest practical change is that equipment origin, vendor control, software, remote access and lifecycle dependencies can now become part of the reliability decision – not just the procurement decision,” Osnato said.
Utilities could have to answer a question beyond whether a piece of equipment works, he said: whether they can continue to rely on it based on who made it, who can access it, what software it depends on and what has changed since it was installed.
Equipment and Software
The order directs the Energy secretary to identify bulk-power system equipment that may pose the risks outlined in the order and prepare recommendations for addressing those risks. DOE also must publish rules to implement the order.
The scope extends beyond physical grid equipment to associated software, firmware and digital capabilities that could create cybersecurity or operational risks.
“The risk is not limited to the metal sitting in a substation,” Osnato said.
The administration is treating foreign supply-chain exposure as a national-security and continuity-of-service issue, rather than simply a trade concern, Osnato said.
The risks include potential cyber or remote-access vulnerabilities inside equipment as well as dependence on foreign suppliers for replacement parts, maintenance, software updates or continued availability, he said.
But determining that risk at the equipment and system level could prove more complicated than identifying where a piece of equipment was manufactured.
“A country-of-origin label alone does not tell an operator whether the full dependency chain is safe,” Osnato said.
NERC said supply-chain security is a critical and evolving issue for grid reliability and security.
The North American Electric Reliability Corp. said its Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center shares actionable information with industry each day on geopolitical and supply-chain security threats targeting the electricity sector.
NERC is also enhancing its supply-chain risk management standard and will work with DOE, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Electricity Subsector Coordinating Council and industry as the administration implements the order, a NERC spokesperson told Data Center Knowledge.
NERC “commends the Administration for the collaborative approach” outlined in the executive order, the spokesperson said.
The order covers a broad range of electric supply-chain equipment, including transformers, generators, inverters, batteries, turbines and control systems. Agencies also can consider associated software, firmware, remote-access capabilities, lifecycle maintenance, update mechanisms and other supply-chain dependencies.
An Aug. 27 Jefferies equity research note said the order reaches an electricity equipment market already facing elongated lead times and sourcing risks tied to AI and data center development.
The analysts expect the restrictions could contribute to longer lead times and higher domestic pricing, while noting that key implementation details remain unresolved until DOE issues its rules.
The order also creates potential complications for equipment already installed or acquired before it was issued, particularly around servicing, retrofits and replacement. Jefferies said accelerated replacement could further extend lead times.
The order requires DOE to consider reliability, safety, replacement availability and continuity of essential service when determining how compliance is phased in.
Data Center Power
For data center developers and operators, the equipment implications come as power availability and infrastructure timelines have become major constraints on new projects.
Jefferies said the equipment targeted by the order already faces elongated lead times and sourcing risks tied to AI and data center development.
That puts equipment procurement directly into the timeline for bringing new data center capacity online. A transformer or other critical component that cannot be sourced, qualified or replaced on schedule can delay a project even when generation and transmission capacity are available.
Osnato said the challenge will be making sure supply-chain requirements are addressed early enough that they do not create problems late in a project.
“The answer should not be to weaken the verification standard,” Osnato said. “It should be to make the evidence standard clearer and earlier in the process so projects do not reach construction or energization before someone discovers that a critical equipment or supply-chain assumption cannot be relied on.”
The administration’s implementation rules will determine how the order affects specific equipment, suppliers and projects. DOE has 120 days to publish rules operationalizing the order.
For utilities and data center developers, that leaves an open question over how much additional scrutiny will be required before critical equipment can be ordered, installed and placed into service.
“Announced equipment availability is not the same as executable, reliable equipment availability,” Osnato said.
And after equipment is approved, he said, the next question is: “What changed since it was approved?”

candidates.title: Warsh furthers his push toward a ‘quieter Fed’
candidates.what_happened: In his first Jackson Hole address, new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh doubled down on a promise to cut “forward guidance” and a commitment to 2% inflation.

facts.name: company
facts.evidence_span: In his first month as Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh indicated

sources.retrieved_text:
In his first month as Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh indicated the central bank would talk less – particularly about what it predicts for future economic conditions – and concentrate more on bringing inflation down.
At the 100-day mark of Warsh’s tenure – coinciding with the Kansas City Fed’s annual Jackson Hole summit in Wyoming – those throughlines remain true.
“You can call it an outline. You can call it a trail map. Just don't call it forward guidance,” Warsh said Friday of his own remarks.
Warsh has made it a point to mute “forward guidance” from the start of his term. In June, at his first Federal Open Market Committee meeting as chair, Warsh oversaw the removal of wording in a previous policy statement that may have suggested the Fed anticipated trimming borrowing costs in the future.
He echoed that stance Friday.
“Transparency in communications about future policy decisions is not a virtue unto itself,” he said. “Communications must be in service to the Fed's paramount responsibility: getting monetary policy right.”
A “quieter Fed,” Warsh said, “is better able to meet its objectives. And we can be held accountable for delivering on our remit: the only true test of our credibility.”
Warsh said the Fed began pushing forward guidance during the 2007-08 financial crisis but that the practice had “overstayed its welcome.”
“Market participants will always try to anticipate what we will do next. But we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade,” Warsh said. “If markets rely materially on the Fed's guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we are all more likely to be blinded to new developments, more likely to be caught unprepared for a turn of events, and more likely to commit errors in policymaking.”
Cutting forward guidance would help “get the relationship right between financial markets and the central bank,” Warsh said.
“The Fed needs clear market signals, as unfiltered as possible, from market internals,” he said. “Market participants … should be tracking real information across the economy. They should draw their own conclusions; form their own expectations of output, employment and inflation; and stay sharply attuned to risks.”
For its part, the Fed “will endeavor to construct more reliable models and more robust rules to guide policy decisions,” Warsh said.
“We'll do this knowing that accuracy in economic forecasting is still just an aspiration,” he added. “With so much changing so fast in geopolitics, global supply chains, and technology, it's wise to be modest about what we can and cannot know.”
On what the Fed can and can’t yet know, Warsh spoke some on the advent of artificial intelligence and its impact on the economic infrastructure.
“It's not obvious where the returns on capital will land or on what timescale,” Warsh said. “Likewise, we don't yet know the equilibrium price of the tokens.”
But, he added, the Fed “will be thinking through these matters with the help of a task force on productivity and jobs.”
“Their recommendations will come later and have no bearing on decisions we make in the current policy conjuncture,” Warsh said. “But I believe that for future policy challenges, this intellectual investment today will leave us far better prepared.”
Warsh noted, too, the amount of time that inflation has hovered above the Fed’s stated 2% target.
“The responsibility for 65 months of sustained, elevated inflation sits squarely with the central bank,” he said. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.”
